screens.title: `distutils`: Python's Original Packaging Tool
screens.narratorSegment: To truly appreciate modern Python packaging, we need to understand its roots. The foundation was laid by the distutils module, which has been a part of Python's standard library since version 1.6. distutils was groundbreaking for its time, providing the basic infrastructure for building and installing Python packages. It introduced the concept of a setup dot P Y file script, which is a Python file that describes your project using a setup open parenthesis close parenthesis function. This function allowed developers to specify basic metadata like the package name, version, and author, along with a list of modules or packages to include. For example, you could define a simple package and then run python setup dot P Y file sdist to create a source distribution, which is essentially a tarball or zip file containing your source code and the setup dot P Y file script. Users could then download this sdist and build the package themselves. However, distutils had significant limitations; it lacked crucial features like automatic dependency management, the ability to define command-line entry points, or support for pre-built binary distributions, making it quite basic for complex projects.

content.html:
Module 11›Chapter 11.1›`distutils` Overview

What is `distutils`?

  • Part of Python's standard library since v1.6.
  • Provides basic infrastructure for package building.
  • Introduced the `setup.py` script and `setup()` function.

Key Limitations

  • No automatic dependency management.
  • No support for command-line entry points.
  • No support for pre-built binary distributions (wheels).
  • Required manual compilation for users.

`distutils` Workflow

Source Code + `setup.py`
Source Distribution (sdist)`.tar.gz` or `.zip`

Users would then run `python setup.py install` to build and install locally.

Key Takeaway

`distutils` provided the initial framework for Python packaging, enabling basic source distributions but lacking modern features like dependency management.

Module 11›Chapter 11.1›`setuptools` Evolution

`distutils` (Foundation)

  • Basic `setup.py` script.
  • Creates source distributions (sdist).
  • Limited metadata and features.

`setuptools` (Extension & Standard)

  • Extends `setup()` with more arguments.
  • Manages external dependencies (`install_requires`).
  • Defines console scripts (`entry_points`).
  • Creates pre-built wheel distributions (`.whl`).
  • Automatic package discovery (`find_packages`).

Key `setuptools` Advantages

Dependency Management

Automatically installs required libraries.

Console Scripts

Define executable commands for users.

Wheel Distributions

Faster, pre-built binary packages.

Package Discovery

Automatically finds packages in your project.

Key Takeaway

`setuptools` significantly advanced Python packaging by adding crucial features like dependency management, entry points, and efficient wheel distributions.

content.html:
Module 11›Chapter 11.1›`setup.py` Anatomy
from setuptools import setup, find_packages

# Read the long description from README.md
with open("README.md", "r", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    long_description = fh.read()

setup(
    name="my-math-utils-cohortia", # Unique package name
    version="0.1.0", # Semantic versioning recommended
    author="Your Name",
    author_email="your.email@example.com",
    description="A simple utility package for basic mathematical operations.",
    long_description=long_description,
    long_description_content_type="text/markdown",
    url="https://github.com/yourusername/my-math-utils",
    packages=find_packages(), # Automatically find packages
    classifiers=[
        "Programming Language :: Python :: 3",
        "License :: OSI Approved :: MIT License",
        "Operating System :: OS Independent",
    ],
    python_requires='>=3.7',
)

Key `setup()` Arguments

  • `name`: Unique package identifier on PyPI.
  • `version`: Current version of the package (e.g., `1.0.0`).
  • `author`, `author_email`: Contact information.
  • `description`: Short summary of the package.
  • `long_description`: Detailed project description, often from `README.md`.
  • `url`: Project homepage or repository link.
Key Takeaway

The `setup.py` script, calling `setuptools.setup()`, is crucial for defining your package's metadata and configuration, acting as its central blueprint.

screens.title: Including Your Code: `packages` Argument
screens.narratorSegment: One of the most critical aspects of your setup dot P Y file file is telling setuptools which parts of your project actually constitute the Python package to be distributed. This is primarily handled by the packages argument within the setup open parenthesis close parenthesis function. You could manually list every package directory, but that quickly becomes tedious and error-prone for larger projects. This is where setuptools. find underscore packages open parenthesis close parenthesis comes to the rescue. This utility function automatically discovers all Python packages within your project directory, making the process much more convenient and less prone to human error. Remember, for a directory to be recognized as a Python package, it must contain an init dot P Y file file. This file, even if empty, signals to Python and setuptools that the directory should be treated as a package. A common mistake is forgetting to include these init dot P Y file files or incorrectly specifying the packages argument, which can lead to parts of your code being omitted from the final distribution. Always double-check your package structure and the packages argument to ensure everything is included as intended.

content.html:
Module 11›Chapter 11.1›Package Discovery

The `packages` Argument

  • Specifies which Python packages (directories) to include.
  • Crucial for `setuptools` to know what to bundle.
  • Can be a manual list, but `find_packages()` is preferred.

`setuptools.find_packages()`

  • Automatically discovers all Python packages in the project.
  • Looks for directories containing `__init__.py` files.
  • Simplifies `setup.py` and reduces configuration errors.

The Role of `__init__.py`

Signals a Python Package

An `__init__.py` file (even empty) tells Python that a directory should be treated as a package.

Common Pitfall

Forgetting `__init__.py` or incorrect `packages` argument can lead to missing code in your distribution.

Key Takeaway

The `packages` argument, often populated by `find_packages()`, is essential for `setuptools` to correctly identify and include all Python packages, relying on `__init__.py` files.

screens.title: Organizing Your Package
screens.narratorSegment: A well-structured project is fundamental for successful packaging. Let's look at a common and recommended directory layout that setuptools can easily understand and process. At the root of your project, you'll typically find the setup dot P Y file file, along with documentation like README. md and licensing information in LICENSE. The core of your application resides within a directory that shares the same name as your package, for example, my underscore package slash. Inside this main package directory, you'll have your init dot P Y file file, which marks it as a Python package, along with your primary modules like module underscore a dot P Y file. If your package has further organization, you'll create subpackages, each containing its own init dot P Y file file, such as subpackage slash module underscore b dot P Y file. It's also good practice to keep your tests in a separate tests slash directory, outside the main package, as they are not part of the distributable code. This clear hierarchy ensures that setuptools can automatically discover and include all the necessary components of your project when building your package.

content.html:
Module 11›Chapter 11.1›Project Structure

Example Project Layout

my_package/
├── my_package/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── module_a.py
│   └── subpackage/
│       └── __init__.py
│       └── module_b.py
├── tests/
│   └── test_module_a.py
├── setup.py
├── README.md
└── LICENSE

Key Components Explained

  • `my_package/`: The main Python package, containing your modules.
  • `__init__.py`: Essential for Python to recognize directories as packages.
  • `setup.py`: The configuration script for `setuptools`.
  • `README.md`, `LICENSE`: Project documentation and legal information.
  • `tests/`: Separate directory for unit tests, not part of the distribution.
Key Takeaway

A clear and consistent project structure, with `__init__.py` files marking packages, is vital for `setuptools` to correctly identify and bundle your code.

screens.title: External Libraries: `install_requires`
screens.narratorSegment: Almost every Python project relies on external libraries. How do you ensure that when someone installs your package, all its necessary dependencies are also automatically installed? This is handled by the install underscore requires argument within your setup open parenthesis close parenthesis function. This argument takes a list of strings, where each string represents a dependency. For example, if your package needs the requests library, you would include 'requests' in this list. You can also specify version constraints, which is a best practice to ensure compatibility. For instance, 'requests is greater than or equal to 2.25.1' means 'requests' version 2.25.1 or newer, while 'numpy' without a version implies any version is acceptable. setuptools will then use this information to automatically fetch and install these dependencies from PyPI when your package is installed. Failing to specify install underscore requires correctly is a common source of installation errors for users, as their environment might lack the necessary libraries for your package to function. Source distributions (`sdist`) bundle your raw code and `setup.py`, requiring local building, making them suitable for inspection but less ideal for quick end-user installation.

Wheel distributions (`.whl` files) are pre-built binary packages that offer significantly faster and more reliable installation for end-users, making them the preferred modern format.
